idiom_name: interface Mediator { void notify(Object sender, Event e); } + colleagues holding it
implementation_notes: Plain Java: declare a Mediator interface with one notification method, implement the coordination in a concrete class (the dialog or controller that knows its colleagues as fields), and let colleagues keep a Mediator reference and report events instead of calling peers. It needs no framework and stays the clearest form when the collaboration itself is the design. For pure fan-out without coordination, the JDK's java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport already supplies the hub's notification half: it manages a listener list and dispatches PropertyChangeEvent objects to registered listeners, so bean-style code does not have to re-implement listener bookkeeping.
pitfalls: Holding concrete colleague types in the mediator compiles but hard-wires the collaboration; interface-typed colleagues keep the hub replaceable and testable.
PropertyChangeSupport fires listeners on the calling thread and holds them strongly: on Swing/JavaFX move work off the UI thread and remove listeners on dispose, or they leak with the hub.
A listener list guarded by nothing is not thread-safe; if the hub is shared across threads, copy-on-write the list (CopyOnWriteArrayList) or synchronise dispatch.

variants.name: Guava EventBus hub
variants.implementation_notes: Guava's EventBus is Java's off-the-shelf in-process mediator: subscribers register themselves, methods annotated @Subscribe declare which event types they handle, and post(event) routes the event to every matching subscriber by runtime type - hub, listener registry and type-based routing are all supplied. Use it when the coordination is event fan-out and no hand-written hub is wanted; subclass AsyncEventBus with an Executor when posting must not block the producer. For request/response coordination with validation, ordering or replies, write the classic mediator instead, because EventBus routes by type only and knows nothing about your protocol.
pitfalls: Routing is by runtime type and an event with no subscriber disappears silently; subscribe a handler for DeadEvent to see dropped messages.
An exception thrown by a @Subscribe method propagates to the poster and stops delivery to the remaining subscribers of that event; AsyncEventBus changes both the thread and the error path.
Registered objects are held strongly, so failing to unregister keeps the subscriber and its UI references alive for the hub's lifetime.
Reflection-based dispatch is slower than a direct virtual call, and a method missing @Subscribe fails silently instead of at compile time.
